extract:
Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers formed in 1976, though their roots lie in Gainesville, Florida, where Tom Petty, guitarist Mike Campbell and keyboardist Benmont Tench had played together in the band Mudcrutch during the early 1970s. Mudcrutch relocated to Los Angeles and signed with Denny Cordell's Shelter Records, but it soon dissolved. Petty then reassembled Campbell and Tench with fellow Gainesville musicians Ron Blair on bass and Stan Lynch on drums. The group remained active for four decades, until Petty's death in October 2017.

Petty's formative influences were the British Invasion bands, especially the Beatles and the Rolling Stones, along with the chiming twelve-string sound of the Byrds, the songwriting of Bob Dylan, and the Southern rock and R&B he absorbed in Florida. Their self-titled 1976 debut on Shelter sounded lean and urgent enough to be loosely grouped with the emerging new wave. It gained traction first in Britain before "Breakdown" and "American Girl" broke through at home. You're Gonna Get It! (1978) consolidated that momentum with "I Need to Know" and "Listen to Her Heart."

After a bitter contractual dispute that involved Petty declaring bankruptcy, the band moved to MCA's Backstreet imprint. There they made Damn the Torpedoes (1979), co-produced with Jimmy Iovine. Its singles "Refugee" and "Don't Do Me Like That" made it a multi-platinum breakthrough. Hard Promises (1981) followed, featuring "The Waiting" and a duet with Stevie Nicks, "Insider." Howie Epstein replaced Blair on bass for Long After Dark (1982), which yielded "You Got Lucky." Southern Accents (1985), partly produced with Dave Stewart of Eurythmics, gave the band "Don't Come Around Here No More," whose Alice in Wonderland video became an MTV staple. The live album Pack Up the Plantation followed later that year. The band then backed Bob Dylan on tour in the mid-1980s and released Let Me Up (I've Had Enough) in 1987.

Petty's solo album Full Moon Fever (1989), made with Jeff Lynne, and his stint in the Traveling Wilburys alongside Dylan, George Harrison, Roy Orbison and Lynne broadened his profile. Lynne went on to produce the band's Into the Great Wide Open (1991), featuring "Learning to Fly" and the title track. A move to Warner Bros. brought collaboration with Rick Rubin, who produced Petty's solo Wildflowers as well as the Heartbreakers' soundtrack She's the One (1996) and Echo (1999). Steve Ferrone took over on drums in the mid-1990s. The Last DJ (2002) delivered a pointed critique of the corporate music industry.

Critics consistently praised the band's craftsmanship, economy and live power, and they became one of the defining acts of American album-oriented rock radio. The group was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2002 and headlined the Super Bowl halftime show in 2008. Songs like "American Girl," "Refugee" and "Free Fallin'" remain fixtures of classic rock radio and film soundtracks.

The band's final album was Hypnotic Eye (2014), and their 40th anniversary tour ended at the Hollywood Bowl just a week before Petty died in 2017. Since then, archival projects have extended the catalog, including the expanded Wildflowers & All the Rest and live collections. Campbell has continued with his band the Dirty Knobs, and Tench remains an in-demand session player. The band's legacy endures as a model of the durable, songwriter-driven American rock band.
title: Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers
